title: researchED Canberra 2026 Reflections
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: A second, independent recap of the inaugural researchED Canberra conference — written by a different attendee than the disruptive educator's already-archived account — covering an almost entirely different set of breakout sessions. Where the companion piece focused on Greg Ashman's and Jenny Donovan's keynotes plus Sarah Siakew and Brendan Lee's breakouts, this writer's day centered on writing and literacy instruction specifically: Jeanette Breen on aligning writing vertically and horizontally across a whole school, Melanie Henry's evidence-informed checklist for auditing literacy intervention in Australian secondary schools (drawn from a two-school pilot of 10 classes and 9 teachers), Jessica Collau Terradas's research on morphological knowledge and adolescent spelling (finding that 83% of a 260-student sample misspelled "indestructible"), and a session on evidence-based critical-thinking instruction in science and humanities that pushes back on generic "think like a historian" framing. The piece closes with Jenny Donovan's keynote on why writing must be taught explicitly and systematically, reinforcing several of the same AERO-derived arguments the companion recap covered but through different quotes and framing, including her point that vocabulary instruction responsibility extends well beyond English teachers into every subject area.
points: Melanie Henry's evidence-informed checklist study, piloted across 2 schools, 10 classes and 9 teachers, found specific literacy-intervention setup choices that worked — no teacher desk (lectern instead), rows with floor markings, preloaded vocabulary aligned with English units — while stressing that intervention "relies on a knowledgeable driver."

Jessica Collau Terradas's research found spelling influences writing quality and assessment outcomes, but that morphological knowledge specifically did not predict spelling accuracy beyond lexical, phonological and orthographic factors in her study of over 260 Year 7 students — where 83% misspelled "indestructible."

The critical-thinking session argued that instructing students to "think like a historian" or "think like a scientist" is pedagogically hollow, since deliberate practice building toward a skill differs fundamentally from generic practice of the end-state task (e.g., exam questions) without the underlying knowledge.

Ashman's point that cognitive load theory is really about long-term memory, not working memory, reframes automaticity-building (rehearsing facts and procedures until they require minimal conscious attention) as the mechanism that frees working memory for genuinely novel problems.

Donovan's keynote places vocabulary-teaching responsibility outside the English department by design: "English teachers do not have the responsibility to teach your subject's vocabulary... responsibility rests as much on secondary cross-disciplinary teachers."
quotes: Put simply, the science of learning is the cognitive science of how students learn, connected with the instructional implication of that science.

This is because the more information we are able to transfer into our seemingly endless long term memory with a strong retrieval strength then we are able to alleviate the burden on working memory to be able to focus on other unique items.

We have so many different types of curriculum between the recommended, written, taught, learned, supported, assessed and hidden but the learned curriculum is what most students remember and can use and therefore it is the most important.

It was found that some of the following worked well: having no teacher desk (and having a lectern instead), rows with floor markings, preloaded vocab in intervention aligned with the English units as well as students being withdrawn from languages or electives.

In this study there were words with very interesting results in the study of over 260 year 7 students. The word 'indestructible' has 83% of students spell it incorrectly while the word infrastructure had 82 unique misspellings.
Sadly, the results of Jess's study showed that morphological factors did not predict spelling accuracy beyond lexical, phonological and orthographic factors.
English teachers do not have the responsibility to teach your subjects vocabulary.... responsibility rests as much on secondary cross disciplinary teachers
